articles.title: Judge halts construction on Trump’s arch — right after a federal panel approved it
articles.summary: Washington — A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from beginning construction on President Trump's proposed triumphal arch late Thursday, siding — for now — with a group of Vietnam veterans and the District of Columbia and Virginia, which sued to stop the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled in a brief order that the government cannot start any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, while further legal proceedings play out. She said she would explain her reasoning in a forthcoming opinion. The ruling came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve plans for the 250-foot triumphal arch, giving the final go-ahead for the monument that's set to be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents. Chutkan's order aside, it's unclear how soon construction of the arch could start, though the Justice Department said in a court filing last month that it could begin as soon as Thursday. In a separate filing Wednesday night, the Trump administration said that a construction company "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval" at the site. Ahead of the meeting, the NCPC's executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approval of the final site and building plans for the structure, which is supposed to celebrate 250 years of American independence. Paoletta, the top lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, heralded Mr. Trump's "historic vision" for the structure and said it would be the "grandest arch ever built by mankind." But California Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said during the hearing that the arch is "illegal" and would "disrupt the solemn connection" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. "This arch would dishonor America, our ideals, and our laws," Huffman said during remarks to the planning commission, adding that Congress is the appropriate body for debating the proposed monument. One Marine veteran who spoke in opposition to the proposal, Jimi Shaughnessy, said "a dominating arch with a carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses is abhorrent and insulting to those who gave all and to their families." "Instead of focusing on the issues facing military families, this administration is intent on spending taxpayer dollars to site, plan, and design a monument no one asked for, and are content with bypassing any laws or regulations that may prevent them from breaking ground," he said. The arch itself will be 166 feet tall and topped with "three gilded figures" — a gold, winged female figure flanked by a gold flying eagle on each side — bringing its overall height to 250 feet, according to documents filed with the NCPC. The structure will sit close to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, though the Federal Aviation Administration determined it will pose "no hazard to air navigation," with a "condition for safety lighting that includes a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting." The arch will also feature an observation deck, and the Trump administration has estimated that it could draw between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors each day. It's expected to take three years to build the arch, which will be located in the center of what is called Memorial Circle, across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial. It's unclear how much the project will cost, and who will foot the bill. Mr. Trump said in September that his "Triumphal Arch" would be a "top grade Military Complex" and house drones and sniper ammunition. But the documents from the NCPC do not include the military usage. Lawyers for the Justice Department declined to provide more details about the national security features in an October hearing. The commission received more than 1,300 public comments about the project, most of which were in opposition, it said. The NCPC's approval comes as Chutkan weighs how to act. A group of Vietnam War veterans, as well as the Commonwealth of Virginia and the city of Washington, D.C., have filed lawsuits arguing that the Trump administration is acting without congressional authorization and is not complying with the required procedures to construct the monument. In an order Tuesday, Chutkan required the government to provide her notice within one hour of any NCPC vote and a thirty-minute notice to any preparation for construction of the arch to give her time to issue a decision on whether to block construction. The government filed the required notices late Thursday, and Chutkan responded by issuing a temporary restraining order that blocked "construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at the site. In a hearing last month, Chutkan said the most important issue for her is whether the Vietnam War veterans had the legal right to sue. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court found that a group of plaintiffs who brought a similar suit to block the White House ballroom construction likely did not have legal standing to challenge the project. In court filings, the Justice Department called the plaintiffs' motions "breathless" and urged Chutkan to follow the Supreme Court's decision in the White House ballroom case, but attorneys for the groups of plaintiffs argued that their legal arguments were different than the ballroom case and urged Chutkan to halt the arch's construction. Two of the plaintiffs, Vietnam veterans Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told Chutkan in a hearing last month that the arch construction would impact their experience when visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery, and said they would be harmed by the arch's size and purpose. In a separate suit brought in late October, Virginia and the District of Columbia sued, and the case was assigned to Chutkan, who had heard arguments the day before from the Vietnam veterans group. The state's attorneys general argued that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm" on them because "the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges." articles.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: Comedian Russell Brand at Southwark Crown Court in London. Anadolu via Getty Images A jury in London found comedian and actor Russell Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The actor had been charged on seven counts: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of attempted indecent assault. Following Thursday's verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women. "The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said in a statement. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims. Following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, the jury found Brand guilty on four of the charges. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. He is due to be sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Nov. 9. The judge said he should expect a lengthy prison term. Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year. He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012. The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but all of them came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women. Russell Brand was accompanied by his wife, Laura, during the trial. Neil Mockford via Getty Images During the trial, the court heard tearful and forceful testimony from the six complainants, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity. The convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a victim who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his gigs. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004. He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin. A third complaint of sexual assault was upheld when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her. Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will. CCTV footage released by the Metropolitan Police shows Brand being interviewed by police in custody in December 2023. "As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing,” Brand can be seen saying. “I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.” He said he did “not recall the names” of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, “However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined." Following the verdict, the judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody. "You've been convicted of a number of offenses including rape," judge Joel Bennathan said. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody." In a statement, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said: "Today's verdict is first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them." The statement added: "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be." Ron Brand, Russell's father, told the BBC he was "shocked" by the verdicts. "I just didn't expect this - it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating." articles.title: Republicans face a crowded agenda and little time before handing Congress to Democrats
articles.summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are on the clock. They have less than two months left in power before the new, Democrat-led Congress is sworn in and their window of unified control in Washington, D.C., comes to an end. Even as the votes are still being counted, GOP leaders have been putting together plans for what they hope to accomplish before they lose power. “Our job is nowhere close to being finished yet,” House Speaker Mike Johnson reportedly told attendees at a watch party Tuesday night as Democratic victories piled up. The period between the November election and the day in early January when new lawmakers are sworn in, often called the “lame duck” session, can be quite productive as lawmakers move with urgency to get things done while they still can. Some of the most important actions taken by Congress in modern history — the legislative response to the Watergate scandal, the Clinton impeachment, the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and several Supreme Court confirmations — all happened during various lame duck windows. Republicans will have a long list of priorities when Congress reconvenes on Monday, but there are also plenty of potential hurdles that could hinder their progress. Here’s a look at what congressional Republicans want to do and some of the possible curveballs that could derail their plans. What needs to get done Congress will have two “must-pass” items on its agenda when it gets back to work next week: avoiding another government shutdown and passing an annual defense policy bill. Leaders from both parties say they want to get both bills done, but disagreement on the specifics could make for a bumpy and time-consuming process. The government will shut down again on Dec. 12 if Congress doesn’t pass a funding bill to keep it open. After enduring the two longest shutdowns in history over the past two years, neither party appears eager to let another one happen. The big point of disagreement could be timing. Republican leaders are reportedly eyeing a bill that would lock in current spending levels for a full year, but Democrats have an incentive to advocate for a short-term bill that sets them up to enact their own spending priorities once they’re in full control of Congress. Negotiations over the defense budget could be even thornier. The Trump administration has asked Congress for $1.5 trillion in military funding for 2027. Democrats have balked at that number, demanding that the price tag be reduced by hundreds of billions of dollars. Reports suggest that the administration may be open to shrinking its budget request, but landing on a final number that both parties and the president can agree on could prove challenging — particularly if the White House insists on including more funding for the war with Iran. “I don't know what [Trump’s] going to want. I don't know how we're going to figure out the money. So no, I don't have easy answers to that,” Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, told Politico on Wednesday. Even if both bills eventually get passed, drawn-out negotiations could eat up precious time and leave little room for Congress to do much else before the end of the year. Republicans’ ‘Last Supper’ In the wake of Tuesday’s losses, some Republican lawmakers have begun advocating for their party to pass one last major budget bill jam-packed with GOP priorities. To do that, they’d need to use the same process they utilized to pass Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, which creates a pathway to circumvent the Senate filibuster and approve legislation without any Democratic votes. “It’s time to wake up and smell the coffee,” Trump adviser Jason Miller told GOP lawmakers on Wednesday. “You have one job. Get everything on President Trump’s agenda through in the limited days we have.” Before the election, Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno told reporters that he would push for a “giant” spending package during the lame-duck session if the GOP lost both chambers of Congress. “It’ll be the Last Supper,” he said. Actually getting another Republican megabill passed could be a steep challenge. Negotiations over the massive list of complex provisions within the One Big Beautiful Bill took months and consumed big chunks of the congressional calendar. Republicans may also have a numbers problem. Any bill they put forward would need near-unanimous support within their party in both chambers. That includes outgoing senators Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, who have been at odds with the president in the late stages of their time in Congress. Republicans also have other, less ambitious priorities that could be at risk if they dedicate their time and energy to another huge party-line budget bill. One of those priorities is a bipartisan proposal to overhaul the permitting process for energy projects, which would make it easier to build both renewable and fossil fuel infrastructure. There’s also a sweeping slate of reforms to college sports , a number of Trump-nominated judges awaiting confirmation , cryptocurrency legislation and more that could end up on the GOP’s long to-do list. Potential curveballs One of the biggest questions looming over Washington, D.C., since Tuesday is whether any of the Supreme Court’s conservative justices might retire during the lame-duck session. With Democrats pledging to prevent Trump from putting another “right-winger” on the court, this could be a conservative justice’s last chance — potentially for years — to retire with the confidence that their replacement is likely to share their ideology. Neither of the court’s two oldest justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, has given any indication that they’re considering stepping down — in fact, Alito has reportedly been unequivocal about his plans to stay on the bench. But if one of them did, Republicans would be heavily incentivized to put everything else on the back burner to rush the confirmation of their replacement before Democrats gain the power to block Trump’s nominees for the rest of his presidency. Republicans’ calendar may also get scrambled by some of their own outgoing members. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has been a key voice behind the push for disclosures about the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein, has said he plans to force a second vote on the issue before he leaves Congress. Massie has said he’s also planning to introduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced heavy scrutiny for his role in carrying out the war in Iran. Tillis recently told CBS News that Hegseth faces a “reckoning” when Congress reconvenes next week. It’s unclear how much support Massie’s impeachment effort has in the House, but even if it failed, it could consume valuable time Republican leaders would rather spend on other priorities. The same would be true of confirmation hearings for a new defense secretary if reports that Trump is considering firing Hegseth prove to be accurate. articles.title: Too close to call: How the Mississippi Senate race turned into such a nail-biter
articles.summary: Mississippi is one of the reddest states in America, so this year's U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and her Democratic challenger Scott Colom wasn't supposed to be especially close. Now it couldn't be closer. As of Thursday afternoon, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by a mere 1,724 votes, according to the Associated Press. That's just 0.19% of all ballots cast. As a result, the AP has yet to call the contest, even though 96% of the vote is in. Along with Alaska — which also remains too close to call — the outcome in Mississippi will determine whether Democrats can expand their new Senate majority beyond its current size (54 seats) by flipping even more red states than they already have . But Alaska was supposed to be a toss-up . Mississippi wasn't really on the national radar. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a "likely Republican" hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it . Yet, here we are, with Colom edging Hyde-Smith as officials tally the final votes. How did the Mississippi Senate race get so close — and what happens next? Who is Scott Colom? Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus. In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases. Colom gives an update about his Senate race on Nov. 4, 2026 in Jackson, Miss. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination. "I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times . But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ." In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper." Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy. How Colom caught up Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since. There were signs before Tuesday that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%. Hyde-Smith speaks at a campaign event in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. Madison Thorn/Bloomberg via Getty Images Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn. Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from." In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 14 million views on Colom's X account . When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own). She done lost her damn mind. pic.twitter.com/wHPt4PSAob — Scott Colom (@scott_colom) October 13, 2026 In the end, it wasn't enough to give Hyde-Smith a decisive victory on Election Day. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom went to his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices. "I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for." According to preliminary New York Times estimates , Colom performed 19 points better among white Mississippi voters than Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. He won new voters — that is, those who didn't vote in 2024 — by 25 points. What happens next The contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith hasn't been called yet because officials are waiting on two remaining batches of ballots. The first batch comes from 11 counties that have yet to report 10% or more of their returns. The other batch contains affidavit ballots, which were generally cast by people who did not present an acceptable photo ID at the polls or who had been marked as inactive on voter rolls. County clerks in Mississippi have 10 days — in this case, until Nov. 13 — to certify the election. Five of the counties with outstanding ballots have favored Colom, including Hinds County (the most populous in the state). Five have favored Hyde-Smith. One is a toss-up. Any mail ballots from those counties must arrive by Tuesday, Nov. 10, in order to count. As for the affidavit ballots, voters need to validate them with an acceptable ID by the same day: Nov. 10. The Colom campaign has said that roughly 10,000 to 15,000 affidavit ballots were cast this year. Colom's team believes his lead will expand once those affidavit ballots are counted. (It has already grown by more than 1,500 votes since Election Day.) Ahead of Mississippi's March primaries, incorrect Experian information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters — and inactivations have more than doubled in some jurisdictions since then. Discrepancies caused confusion and long lines at polling places on Tuesday, forcing affected voters to cast affidavit ballots. "We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat," Colom wrote on X on Wednesday morning . He added on Thursday that "my campaign, alongside the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] and Elias Law Group, Lisa Ross, and our great team of local attorneys, are leading the effort to ensure every eligible voter is heard." Hyde-Smith also expressed confidence on Election Night. "We still don't have all the votes in, so we're not calling all of it tonight, but we're in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator," she told supporters at the time. On Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party chairman Mike Hurst estimated that about 20,000 ballots had not been counted yet. "We are enthusiastic about these outstanding ballots because a number of these, a significant number of these, we believe, are in and remain in Republican-leaning districts, precincts and counties throughout the state," Hurst told reporters. Mississippi is the only state in the country without a recount law. But if the margin is still razor-close next week, Colom or Hyde-Smith could challenge certain ballots in court. That would likely happen after certification on Nov. 13. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith and her campaign have formally written to Mississippi state officials to demand “the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots,” according to the New York Times — a signal that they may pursue litigation if those ballots put Colom over the top. articles.title: Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument, but his gold decor isn't protected
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday. But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors. Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms. "It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself." It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Trump gathered reporters to sign the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark. The proclamation, released after Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character." It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires "documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument." Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text. "If they want to say, 'Let's not have oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen," said Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom. A red baseball cap with "VETO" on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress. His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Trump's ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face "alternative measures to obtain compliance." Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents. As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address "very bad lighting." His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits. Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval. "If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be," Trump said, "and I'll come back here and I'll make sure it never happens." articles.title: Republicans turn against Pete Hegseth after significant midterms losses
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States’ costly and unpopular war with Iran following the historic drubbing Republicans took from Democrats in this week’s midterm elections. But President Trump insisted on Wednesday that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief — at least not yet. “No, I think he’s doing a very good job,” Trump told reporters. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state’s next governor this week. “I think he’s doing a very good job, and I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that. But I haven’t heard that at all,” Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn’s seat. According to CBS News , though, Trump “has been asking advisers” whether Hegseth should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28. Pool via Getty Images Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vice President JD Vance was unequivocal. “The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . “The reason we lost is the war.” The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces “a reckoning.” “He is one of the reasons why we don’t have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need,” Tillis said on election night. “I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress.” Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.” The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Carter/Getty Images When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth’s handling of the military is high on their list. “In the majority, one of the first things we’re gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month . They may not have to wait that long. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky and vocal Trump critic, said he intends to force a House vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution, bypassing Congress on war declarations and unlawful military actions in several countries. Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the Republican primary — introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. In a post on X Wednesday , Massie wrote that "there is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns." A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images Hegseth, for his part, remains defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to his X account on Thursday afternoon, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he’s implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke”) and praised Trump’s leadership while dismissing Massie’s impeachment pursuit. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly,” Hegseth said. “It didn’t work with President Trump and it won’t work with me.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/trump-stands-by-hegseth-after-election-losses-but-other-republicans-want-him-out-163852105.html

articles.title: 'Tax the rich' (mostly) wins in ballot measures across the country
articles.summary: Voters weighed in on tax ballot initiatives across at least 10 states this week, returning verdicts that demonstrate plenty of “tax the rich” sentiment despite the likely failure of California's high-profile plan for a wealth tax. Other successful measures sought to limit taxes on Americans of more modest means either through new caps on state income taxes or lower property taxes. Voters' affordability worries ran, "at least in part, through the tax code," as the Tax Foundation summarized the results in a wrap-up of the races. Californians gather the day after the midterm elections in San Diego, Calif., on Nov. 4. (Reuters/Mike Blake) REUTERS / REUTERS In California, a billionaire tax imposing a one-time 5% wealth tax on state residents and trusts with assets over $1 billion appeared on track to fail , after voters cooled on the effort as the campaign wound down. But proponents of other taxes on the rich counted plenty of wins, including elsewhere on California's ballot. The state's voters approved permanently higher tax rates on incomes starting at $250,000 in a separate measure that solidified rates first approved in 2012 to fund education. Elsewhere in the US, a "millionaires tax" in Washington state survived with 58% of voters rejecting a proposal to repeal a new 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million per year to fund education, healthcare, and other priorities beginning in 2028. Colorado is on track to narrowly pass a measure to raise taxes on its richest residents. That initiative aims to raise rates on incomes above $500,000 and tops out at 8.4% for incomes over $1 million. "In three of four cases, voters showed their support for taxing the rich," the left-leaning Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy said in an analysis of state tax ballot measures , calling it a win for tax fairness. (The California wealth tax initiative and the Colorado measures have not yet been formally called by the Associated Press, so the results could change.) A person receives an "I voted" sticker during the midterm elections in Los Angeles. (Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein) REUTERS / REUTERS A range of measures to limit taxes Elsewhere in the nation, voters put a cap on future tax increases. North Carolina voted to permanently cap state income taxes at 3.5% and approved a second measure to limit property taxes imposed at the local level. Iowa approved its own measure that sets a higher threshold for lawmakers to approve future tax hikes. Utah approved a similar measure making it harder for future voters in the state to raise taxes through ballot initiatives. Florida voters moved on housing costs and approved a phased-in $250,000 homestead exemption to limit property taxes except those used to fund public schools. The vote on Florida's Amendment 3, according to an Associated Press tally , was 62% in favor. Such measures have ripple effects on state budgets for years. The Tax Foundation warned that Florida's move leaves "local governments in the lurch and incentivizes them to raise rates on property still in the tax base or to generate more revenue from less economically efficient taxes." Voters cast ballots at a polling place in Orlando on Nov. 3. (Ronaldo Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto via Getty Images Other states voted to keep things where they are. Massachusetts voters appeared on track to reject an effort to expand the state's so-called revenue limit, which, if approved, could have resulted in smaller tax refunds. Oklahoma rejected a plan this week to change property tax assessment limits. Wyoming voted in a similar direction, rejecting a plan that would have established a new 50% property tax exemption for homeowners. Missouri also rejected a state income tax measure this summer that would have phased it out entirely. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Newsom to commute all 548 California death sentences to life in prison without parole
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at a rally at the Hollywood Palladium on Sunday. (Ariana Drehsler / For The Times) Gov. Gavin Newsom told the California Supreme Court on Thursday that he will commute the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution, reducing their punishments to life in prison without parole. Newsom can commute about 40% of the death sentences with the stroke of a pen, but the rest will require the high court’s approval in order to be finalized. The mass commutation would apply to men and women convicted of some of the most heinous acts in the state’s history. Newsom and other opponents of capital punishment have long argued that the process is costly, cruel and discriminatory, with death sentences disproportionately handed down to defendants of color. “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundation of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians explaining his decision . “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.” The move comes in Newsom’s final months as governor and as he considers a run for president. Reducing the death sentences could help him in a primary with a Democratic base of like-minded liberal voters, but potentially hurt him in a general election with a national electorate that supports capital punishment. The decision to officially spare the condemned inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs every year. Only 13 inmates have been killed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The state’s electorate reaffirmed its support a decade ago, voting down a ballot initiative that would have abolished capital punishment. Polls show its popularity has waned in the years since. Despite his outspoken opposition to state-sanctioned executions, the governor has declined to use his political influence with voters to pursue a ballot measure that would amend the state Constitution to align with his position and officially end the death penalty. Without changing state law, criminals can continue to be sentenced to death in California. “California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books and I respect that,” Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. “But the Constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment.” Newsom made national headlines two months after his inauguration in 2019 when he issued a temporary moratorium on executions and vowed to dismantle the death chamber at San Quentin State Prison, now called San Quentin Rehabilitation Center. Calling the death penalty system a “failure,” Newsom said the punishment is also often reserved for poor people who cannot afford expensive legal representation, fails to deter crime and wastes taxpayer money. Careful to avoid elevating a death penalty debate in the midterm elections, Newsom intentionally waited until after the general election on Tuesday to go a step further and launch the process of commuting all California death penalty sentences. The decision is another bold signature Newsom move that sits well with his base of support in California and wealthy, white and college-educated national voters who would be crucial to his success in a Democratic presidential primary, said Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant. “Gavin’s exactly right with that base Democratic voter on that position,” Madrid said. “One hundred percent. It makes him a champion.” However, his liberal stance on government executions could also create a vulnerability for him if he advances in the 2028 presidential election as the party’s nominee. More moderate blue-collar voters who helped the party flip Congress in the midterms, Madrid added, are “not in line with him on this.” A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted  of murder. Those numbers could shift following the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s now-scuttled plan to livestream the execution of Ft. Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad. “Those events have really ripped the veneer off the death penalty in this country,” said attorney Natasha Minsker of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition. “The death penalty is an act of violence. It’s taking another life. I think that’s become clear to the entire country.” The state spends more than $200 million a year to adjudicate automatic death penalty appeals and habeas corpus petitions for inmates who, in all likelihood, will never be executed, according to a 2025 report by the Habeas Corpus Resource Center. The case of Clarence Ray Allen, the last inmate killed by lethal injection in California 20 years ago, is emblematic of how the law has failed, death penalty opponents say. Allen was 76, making him the second-oldest person ever executed in the United States. He had been on death row for 23 years and his appeals cost the state more than $750,000. Many current condemned inmates are even older — some in their 80s and 90s — and their appeals even more drawn-out and expensive. “It’s just a broken system,” said Michael Hersek, former executive director of Habeas Corpus Resource Center and an ex-state public defender. Taxpayers foot the bill for both the defense and the prosecution in post-conviction capital cases, as well as the administrative judicial costs associated with years of complicated appeals in state and federal court. The existing appeal requirements were instituted to counter long-standing racial bias in capital sentencing. Attempts to reform and expedite the appeals process over the years have further gummed up the system. “There is no indication that the situation has improved, and ... [there are] data indicating that it has worsened,” Justice Leondra R. Kruger wrote for the California Supreme Court in 2024. It’s estimated that death penalty appeals alone constitute about a quarter of the work of the California Supreme Court. “It’s ludicrous, the amount of time, resources and energy put into these cases,” Hersek said. Some victims’ families agree. “The death penalty is this promise to people who are angry and broken that you’re somehow going to make them feel better by executing this person,” said Bethany Webb , whose sister Laura was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Seal Beach in 2011. Their mother was also badly injured in the attack. “It is brutalizing to family members, the whole system,” Webb said. More joined the chorus in the wake of the announcement. “The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” said Jess Nichol, whose 12-year-old sister, Polly Klaas, was abducted from their Petaluma home and murdered in 1993, sparking a search that gripped the nation. Others say Newsom’s latest move is a betrayal of the justice they were promised. “It’s total disrespect for the victims. It’s a slap in the face,” said Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son, Michael Lyons, was abducted, raped and murdered in 1996. She and other relatives stressed the unique brutality of many capital crimes, saying Newsom did not consider victims’ suffering when commuting their killers’ sentences. “[Newsom] has a heart for criminals, I don’t think he has a heart for victims,” said Phyllis Loya, whose son, Larry Lasater, a police officer in Pittsburg, Calif., was killed in the line of duty by a man who was sentenced to death. “He doesn’t care about us.” The commutations would go to inmates such as Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing six men, three women and two infant boys in Northern California in 1984 and 1985. Also in line to benefit is Klaas’ killer, Richard Allen Davis, who famously flipped cameras the bird after he was convicted. Another condemned inmate, Christopher Cheary, was convicted of murdering, raping and torturing his girlfriend’s 3-year-old daughter, Sophia Acosta, in Tulare County. Former Sacramento County Dist. Atty. Anne Marie Schubert, the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and a death penalty supporter, said the families of murder victims had been “run over, torn up, and thrown in the garbage” by the commutations. The governor decided that his personal opinion was more important than judges, juries and the will of the voters, she said, questioning why Newsom didn’t take action when he first took office instead of enacting a blanket reprieve on his way out as governor. “It is perhaps the greatest travesty of justice I’ve ever witnessed,” Schubert said. “I think what’s particularly concerning is that the families of murdered children, killed police officers and [victims of] school shooters, mass shooters and baby killers — those families were not even given the decency of a phone call or a meeting or any kind of notice.” Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra also opposes the death penalty. If state leaders wanted to resume executions, experts say it would take the better part of a decade and millions of dollars in new spending for the state to design and approve a workable protocol for lethal injections, rebuild a death chamber and secure the gray-market drugs necessary to perform executions. Legal experts believe the end of the death penalty is likely inevitable in California, with or without Newsom’s involvement. In 2024, the Office of the State Public Defender sued California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office, arguing “persistent and pervasive racial disparities infect California’s death penalty system.” This spring, the California Supreme Court ordered Bonta’s California Department of Justice to show cause why it should not declare the death penalty unconstitutional — a move widely read as signaling the justices’ ultimate intent to end it. “The statistical findings in the studies invoked by petitioners are extraordinarily disturbing,” Bonta wrote in his reply to the order in August. “Evidence of pervasive racial disparities in the administration of the death penalty could show that California’s capital punishment system gives rise to a constitutionally intolerable risk of arbitrariness.” Among the 529 men and 19 women in line for commutations, around 60% would require review and approval by the California Supreme Court before Newsom’s term ends in January. Those cases involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution. The high court previously rejected 10 clemency cases without much clarification when Gov. Jerry Brown submitted them in 2018 months before he left office. If the mass commutation is approved by the California Supreme Court, the immediate effect could be relatively muted. The death chamber was taken down and all but a handful of the remaining condemned inmates were relocated from segregated housing in San Quentin to other facilities across the state after Newsom’s 2019 moratorium. The decision to formally pause executions drew support from the late Pope Francis during Newsom’s 2024 trip to the Vatican, according to the governor’s retelling of a brief conversation between the two men. In a subsequent interview, the governor said his Catholic background and the inequities in the criminal justice system influenced his refusal to sign off on executions. His father, the late William Newsom, also opposed the death penalty. His father and grandfather were involved in the case of Pete Pianezzi, a friend who was wrongfully convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting and killing of a gambler and busboy in Los Angeles in 1937. Pianezzi escaped the death penalty by a single vote and served 13 years in prison. He was later exonerated. Even if it were possible to limit inequity and wrongful convictions in the criminal justice system, Newsom has said he would still be against the death penalty. “The decision is among the most difficult in my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families,” Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. “Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing.” California politics editor Phil Willon contributed reporting. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . articles.title: Trump admin. secretly worked with Iran on deportations during war, records show
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show. The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although they did not specify when that would be carried out. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out. A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement said at least a dozen Iranian detainees had been notified over the past week that they were being deported to Iran, with some told it could be as soon as this coming Sunday. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the new court documents were released. Earlier court filings and emails show the administration held talks with Iran on deportations that took place last year and shortly before the war. But the revelation that it was maintaining those contacts even after the war broke out highlighted the administration's resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees. “We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript. “And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.” “Yes, your honor,” Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.” Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals. The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iran during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal.” The State Department said it generally does not comment on pending litigation or private diplomatic discussions. It referred other questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Lawsuit has been challenging deportations of Iranian asylum seekers The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said Thursday the Iranian detainees were contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. Some had also been notified by DHS officials of the upcoming deportation. One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center where detainees are often sent immediately before a removal. None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said. “Some of those same asylum applicants, and others who could face the same death, are being sent back — all against a backdrop of further and intensifying U.S. bombing of Iran,” Chubin said. “This flight must be stopped.” Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent. The lawsuit on the Iranian asylum seekers alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings state. The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government. The judge overseeing the case said it was possible the government shared the confidential information, but appeared skeptical of claims that have arisen in the lawsuit that DHS has a coordinated policy of sharing those records. In addition, hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026. Deportations of Iranians have been historically rare During the Oct. 15 hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights. “We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” Reyes said. In a court filing Wednesday, the Justice Department said the judge’s order effectively served as an injunction against the government “given the possibility of sanctions and contempt dangling overhead.” Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran. But under the Trump administration, which is carrying out a broad immigration crackdown, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations. Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country, but it has also meant deporting people to other countries they have no connection with. The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won’t take their people back. During Trump’s second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S. In June, an Iranian woman was among two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic. ___ Riddle reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press reporter Matthew Lee contributed to this report. Follow the AP's coverage of the Iran war at https://apnews.com/hub/iran . articles.title: Meghan Markle's half-brother named person of interest in father's abuse case
articles.summary: Meghan Markle's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., is a "person of interest" in an investigation by police in the Philippines into alleged child sexual abuse material linked to their father, Thomas Markle, the country's interior secretary said Thursday. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told reporters at a press conference in Manila that authorities were examining whether Markle Jr., 60, was involved but that he was not currently considered a suspect. "We will know in the next week," he said in a video shared by Reuters. "There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well, but only as a person of interest so far," he said, adding that "he is not currently considered a suspect." Thomas Markle, 82, has been under investigation since October in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. He has not been charged. The Sun first reported that Markle Jr. told Philippine police that after his father left the Philippines in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu. Remulla told AFP on Oct. 24 that police inspected Markle Sr.'s former home in Cebu following a report from his son and found a "trove" of suspected child sexual abuse material and a laptop. Markle Sr. has vehemently denied the allegations against him, telling the British newspaper the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick." In an interview with the Daily Mail , he said the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico in January 2025 and that he did not know who had access to them. He said he would welcome a forensic examination of the devices. In a separate interview with the Daily Mail's sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, he said: "I have never had sex with anyone under the age of 18." He added that if there was anything bad on his devices, "it was put there by someone else," according to the British newspaper the Daily Telegraph . Remulla told the British newspaper the Guardian on Oct. 25 that investigators were considering all angles because the case involved a family dispute, while stressing that a full forensic examination would give a "definitive picture." "We want to be sure before we release the findings," he added. The FBI told Yahoo it was "aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law." What do we know about Thomas Markle Jr.? Thomas Markle Jr., 60, is Meghan's half-brother and the son of Thomas Markle and his first wife, Roslyn Loveless. He has a sister, Samantha Markle. Markle Jr. had been caring for his father in the Philippines, where he reported him to Philippine police. Remulla said police had received information about underage girls reportedly being brought to Markle Jr.'s home in Cordova, in the Philippines. "We have witnesses that underage girls are brought to his house and we are following it up," he said. Shortly after the investigation into his father was announced, Markle Jr. apologized to his sister for siding with their father during their years-long estrangement, telling the Sun on Sunday that he was "so, so sorry." He said: "I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years." Recalling looking after Meghan when she was a child, he asked her to accept his apology and wished her family well. Markle Jr. has not been charged. Meghan was sent letter containing allegations in 2019 After the allegations in the Philippines came to light, Meghan said in a public statement issued on Oct. 23 that she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations that had emerged against her father. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," she said. It subsequently emerged that officers at London’s Metropolitan Police passed on a letter to Meghan in early 2019 that informed of her of allegations about her father. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies. According to British tabloid the Sun on Sunday , Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case. Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them." She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her. According to the Sun on Sunday , and also reported by the BBC and the Daily Telegraph , the Duchess of Sussex sent the letter to Thomas Markle while he was hospitalized in the Philippines following a leg amputation in December 2025 after a blood clot. articles.title: 特朗普：美股经历史上最糟交易日之一，都怪民主党
articles.summary: 美国中期选举结果揭晓后次日，华尔街遭遇今年以来最惨烈的单日抛售，特朗普将矛头直指民主党。 11月5日，纳斯达克综合指数单日暴跌5.52%，标普500指数下挫逾4%，三大股指均创下2025年4月关税冲击以来最大单日跌幅。科技股首当其冲，英伟达、博通、高通等芯片巨头跌幅均超9%，市场对民主党执政后AI政策走向的忧虑成为直接导火索。 特朗普随即在社交媒体连发多文， 将此次暴跌归咎于民主党的中期选举大胜，并以自创词"蠢民主党人"（Dumocrats）直接点名攻击，警告选民"你们只能怪自己"。他同时为共和党执政期间的市场表现辩护，并表示"别担心，我们很快就会以某种方式，变得比以往任何时候都更加强大"。 美股创下关税冲击以来最大单日跌幅 美东时间11月5日收盘，纳斯达克综合指数大跌5.52%，较10月6日创下的历史收盘高点回落逾10%，正式进入技术性回调区间，并创下19个月以来最大单日跌幅。标普500指数和道琼斯工业平均指数同步大幅下挫。 此次抛售造成的财富损耗触目惊心。据估算，标普500指数成分股单日市值蒸发约2.9万亿美元，纳斯达克综合指数成分股缩水2.5万亿美元，科技七巨头合计蒸发市值约1.04万亿美元。普通美国人的401（k）退休账户亦遭受直接冲击。 特朗普表态：归咎民主党，自许"东山再起" 选举结果公布次日，特朗普在Truth Social连发多条帖文，措辞激烈。他写道： "受选举结果影响，股市经历了历史上最糟糕的日子之一。目睹这一切真是令人难过！我们曾付出巨大努力，将经济推向了前所未见的水平，结果却变成了这样。因此，你们的401（k）退休账户缩水了。 记住，这并非共和党所为，而是那些'蠢民主党人'干的。 " 他在另一条帖文中进一步写道： "今天股市崩盘了，因为'蠢民主党人'在周二大获全胜。真是可悲，这只能怪你们自己！我当时根本没在选票上。如果我在选票上，我们早就以压倒性优势获胜了。" 值得注意的是，就在选举结果公布当日——即市场暴跌前一天——特朗普曾在社交媒体发文，就股市盘中上涨自居其功，称"不到两年内就创下91次历史新高，你们的401（k）账户突破天际"。 eToro分析师Jakub Rochlitz对每日邮报表示，选举结果是此次抛售最直接的催化剂，但市场已在此前有所松动——Anthropic和OpenAI的增长数据于10月初令投资者失望，使市场对负面消息的敏感度明显上升。"中期选举结果并没有真正制造新的恐惧，它只是压倒这座本已摇摇欲坠的纸牌屋的最后一阵风，"前高盛分析师Nic Puckrin对每日邮报表示。 分析人士指出， 此次跌幅之深，与当前市场存在大量杠杆资金密切相关。 投资者借入资金入市规模处于历史高位，一旦市场情绪逆转，去杠杆压力将加速并放大跌势。 此前，AI交易是推动美股持续创历史新高的核心主题，科技七巨头估值长期处于高位。随着Anthropic和OpenAI增长数据不及预期，加之中期选举带来的政策不确定性，市场对这一核心叙事的信心开始动摇，估值修正压力随之释放。在当前的高杠杆环境下，这一连锁反应的烈度被进一步放大。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: “一键打包”成三方平台新战略：是抢额度，还是降风险？
articles.summary: 在稳健理财收益走低、跨境配置需求上升的背景下，“一键打包”QDII定投工具悄然兴起。 多家基金代销平台近期集中上线相关服务。投资者可一次勾选多只跟踪纳指、标普500等指数的限购QDII基金，由系统按各基金当日可用额度自动分配、批量扣款，降低单只基金小额限购下逐只买入的操作成本。 何为“一键打包”QDII？ “一键打包”QDII，是基金代销平台推出的批量定投功能：投资者自行选定基金池并设定总预算，系统按各基金当日可用额度自动分配、批量扣款，把“逐只买基金”这一操作环节自动化。平台不替投资者选产品，也不提供配置建议。 操作上，投资者在平台勾选多只跟踪纳指、标普500等指数的QDII基金，设定总预算上限；系统每日扫描各基金剩余额度，有额度即自动分配并扣款，某只基金额度用完则跳过。一次验密后，无需每天手动查额度、逐只下单。 各家平台的规则有所不同。理财通（批量定投纳指）支持一次勾选37只纳指QDII，可以逐只设金额；微众银行（省心定投）覆盖纳指100、标普500、纳指科技、纳指生物等品类，但不支持撤单；且慢（纳指管家）可以按跟踪误差、费率等指标排序，系统按排序依次买入；度小满（省心投）主打一键多投、自动抢额度。 平台规则不同，但能投多少最终仍取决于各基金当日额度。平台密集上线这类工具，背景是海外宽基QDII配置需求持续提升。 海外宽基 QDII 配置需求提升 近期，国内存款利率、银行理财和货币基金收益率持续下行。一年期定存利率已跌破1%，银行理财平均收益率也降至2%以下，稳健类产品的收益空间明显收窄。投资者开始把目光转向海外宽基QDII，将其作为多元化配置的一个方向。2026年上半年，QDII基金净新增持有人户数接近3000万户，在非货基金中排在首位。 纳指这轮回调，进一步推升了海外宽基QDII的配置需求。10月以来纳指自高点回撤近10%，在定投逻辑下，同样的金额能买到更多份额，摊薄成本的效果更明显。部分投资者把回调视为分批买入的窗口，申购意愿集中释放。 但需求升温的同时，供给端并不宽松。QDII外汇额度总量有限，单只纳指基金每天能买的金额从十几元到几百元不等，部分产品只有10元、20元。想按计划完成定投，投资者只能把钱拆到几十只基金里逐只买，操作成本高。 正是在这一供需错位下，“一键打包”QDII工具上线，帮投资者在额度有限的情况下，把几十只基金的买入操作集中完成，省去逐只下单的麻烦。 总额度依然有限 一键打包降低了操作层面的成本，却没有解决额度总量问题。它只是把不同基金公司各自独立的零散额度汇集起来使用，行业总额度并未增加。额度收紧时，扣款失败、定投买不满的情况仍会发生。 工具能在既有额度内把买入流程跑得更顺，但可投多少仍由各基金公司当日释放的规模决定。理财通37只纳指基金合计每日可投约235元，这个数字说明，可选产品再多，可投总量也不会超过各基金当天放出的额度。 一键打包让定投在限购环境下更好执行，但额度没有变多。工具解决的是操作麻烦，额度约束依然存在。 投资风险依然存在 QDII基金本身面临两层波动：一是海外市场波动，纳指涨跌直接反映在净值上；二是汇率波动，人民币兑美元的变动会影响以人民币计价的收益。此外，QDII申赎周期比境内基金更长，到账偏慢，流动性也相对较弱。买入方式变成“一键”，这些风险并不会消失。 除了市场波动，定投计划还面临额度不确定性。各基金公司的QDII额度会动态调整，额度收紧时，工具也无法保证按计划足额买入。一键打包能提高执行效率，但不能保证每期都投满。 此外，一键打包也不等于分散投资。勾选几十只基金，看似分散了资金，但如果这些基金都跟踪同一个指数，底层持仓高度重叠，美股系统性下跌时仍会同步回撤，打包并没有降低资产层面的波动。 对普通投资者来说，一键打包更适合用长期闲钱、以小比例参与全球配置，控制仓位，降低收益预期。使用前也要理性看待这一工具：工具便利不等于投资收益，一键打包优化的是操作体验，不是收益本身。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 油价暴跌20%，金价为何逆势大涨“？高盛：黄金成为"反向石油交易"
articles.summary: 布伦特原油单周暴跌约20%，黄金却同步反弹逾3%——高盛认为，这并非偶然，而是一套贯穿全年的价格机制的集中呈现。 周三，原油单日下跌9%，黄金则录得8月以来最大单日涨幅，涨逾3%，报约4130美元/盎司。 (本周黄金和原油走势分化) 高盛交易员Rich Privorotsky在最新晨报中提出， 黄金已演变为原油的"镜像交易" ：能源进口国央行此前被迫抛售黄金以支付高企的石油账单，随着油价回落，这一强制性卖压边际消退，黄金随即获得支撑。 这一机制同时解释了一个长期困扰市场的悖论：在今年地缘政治风险最为尖锐的时段，黄金并未充当"避险资产"，反而从1月高点逾5600美元大幅回落至4000美元以下。 华尔街见闻观察到，年初以来，金油相关性以负相关为主。 金油20日相关系数一度达到异常高的-0.6，而美伊战前该系数约为+0.6 。 （金油20日相关系数最新约为-0.60，处于年内低位区间） 按高盛的框架，2026年黄金的边际卖方，正是那些急需美元的石油进口国。 油价下跌，美元压力缓解，抛售动力随之减弱。 谁在动用"储蓄罐" 土耳其是最具代表性的案例。 华尔街见闻此前提及 ，战争爆发后两周内，土耳其抛售58吨黄金，动用所得美元同时用于支撑里拉和支付大幅攀升的能源进口账单；此后一周， 累计抛售量翻倍，相当于其全部黄金储备的约15% 。土耳其3月份外汇储备出现有记录以来最大单月降幅，同期还几乎清空了所持美国国债。 （土耳其当时抛售规模相当于其全部黄金库存的约15%，相当于该国过去六年积累的储备规模） 土耳其并非孤例。3月份全球央行整体转为净卖出黄金，为近十个月来首次；俄罗斯亦出售黄金以填补财政缺口，而波兰和中国则维持净买入。 高盛旗下大宗商品研究员Adam Gillard指出， 土耳其及其他新兴市场经济体的集中抛售，是黄金较战前高点暴跌逾1000美元的直接诱因。 油价已在为"和平"定价 Privorotsky同时指出，原油已提前兑现大量利好。 布伦特远期合约价差已首次自7月中旬以来重新转为期货溢价结构，这是一个结构性看跌信号，表明市场预期中东石油供应将持续正常化。部分分析人士认为合理油价已低于70美元。 （布伦特远期合约与现货即期原油价差转负） Privorotsky本人坦言对短期走势"有些担忧，有点担心局势过于乐观，不确定是否会出现周末局势升级"。 对比交易逻辑而言： 继续做空原油（风险更高） ： 原油单周已经大跌了 20%，如果现在还去追空，等于是在赌“中东等地区的和平预期会持续发酵，地缘政治带来的风险溢价会进一步消失”。一旦局势稍有风吹草动，原油很容易报复性反弹。 买入黄金（更稳妥） ： 买黄金是在赌“今年那些迫使新兴市场疯狂抛售资产的压力不会重演”。只要这个压力不爆发，黄金就有支撑；就算局势突然恶化，黄金作为避险资产也能抗跌。 野村证券策略师Charlie McElligott亦从不同角度得出相近结论： 若特朗普对伊朗的强硬立场有所松动，此前来自海湾合作委员会国家及伊朗的黄金卖压也可能同步缓解，海湾地区同样是此轮抛售的参与方，原因与土耳其如出一辙。 黄金市场仓位极度偏空 高盛认为对于考虑追多黄金的投资者，当前仓位结构提供了一个值得关注的信号。 Gillard写道，本轮黄金反弹主要由CTA空头回补及有限规模的中国买盘驱动，"未见明显的宏观资金介入"，机构层面尚未看到实质性的重新布局。 高盛CTA仓位指标已从夏末约+4降至约-7，为两年数据中的最低水平。 （黄金CTA仓位与金价走势对比） ETF层面同样承压。据彭博报道，GLD当月出现6月以来首次资金净流出，规模约18亿美元；Gillard估算， GLD及iShares的持有者均价约在4400美元/盎司附近，较当前价格约高6%，大量被套盘的存在将对初期反弹形成一定阻力 。 （黄金ETF持有者均价约在4400美元/盎司附近） 彭博宏观策略师Simon White则指出，上周五黄金那轮3.7%的急跌"具有流动性补充式抛售的典型特征"，使黄金价格跌破其2023年以来首次失守的合理估值区间。 综合极度偏空的CTA持仓、被套的ETF持有者及低于公允价值的绝对水平，高盛分析师James McGeoch指出， "货币贬值"话题已重回市场讨论，周三未平仓合约上升1%，多头持续加仓 。 结构性买盘从未离场 与此同时，黄金结构性需求实际上并未消失。 世界黄金协会最新数据显示，第三季度央行购金量达321吨，同比增长42%，为2024年以来最快，年初至今累计购入675吨，以中国和波兰央行为主要买家。黄金ETF三季度录得创纪录的310亿美元净流入，总持仓升至历史高点4256吨。 然而，金矿股与金价之间的传导仍存在时滞 。高盛澳大利亚矿业分析师Hugo Nicolaci团队指出，柴油成本仍处于公司指引上沿，尽管近期油价有所回落，燃料成本占全维持成本比例约为1%-10%，短期利润率仍面临压缩风险。 高盛已将澳股Genesis Minerals下调至中性，将Regis Resources下调至卖出，并指出澳洲矿业板块目前隐含金价约3600美元/盎司，低于现货及远期价格的4000美元以上—— 对矿商而言，逆油价红利需等到更低廉的燃料成本切实反映在财报中才能兑现 。 跟着油价账单走，而非美联储 传统分析框架将黄金锚定于实际利率和美元 。 本周美债收益率全线下行、美元因选举结果走软，确实构成利好，但这一框架无法解释黄金为何在地缘政治风险最高涨时大幅下挫。 油价通过新兴市场央行的抛售行为，始终是本轮黄金边际定价的真正驱动力 。 （金油比回到40倍上方） 从这里出发，市场面临两条路径： 其一 ，局势降温延续，能源账单下降，土耳其等央行停止净抛售并最终回购此前变现的黄金，CTA翻多，金价向4400美元均价乃至更高水平回归； 其二 ，地缘冲突再度升温，油价反弹，新兴市场储备压力重来。 Privorotsky认为，做多黄金是"更具防御性"的降温交易，同时也是更好的货币贬值对冲工具。 后一逻辑在于，新一届国会被预期重启财政扩张，赤字上行路径清晰，这正是"货币贬值"一词重回市场话语的根本原因。 articles.title: 创业板跌3.5%，AI硬件领跌、“易中天”再度集体调整，光伏、农业逆势活跃，恒指、恒科指均跌超1%
articles.summary: 隔夜美股遭遇大跌，科技股重创， 纳指重挫超5% ，芯片指数跳水12%，拖累亚太市场，日本和韩国股市周五早盘双双杀跌，三星电子、SK海力士下挫，A股和港股低开低走，AI硬件股跌幅居前，“易中天”齐跌。午盘，中际旭创、新易盛、立讯精密、东山精密、天孚通信、海光信息等上市公司纷纷在午间发布公告，表态将充分运用政策工具，通过回购等方式，维护公司价值和广大投资者利益。 11月6日，A股早盘大幅低开，三大股指盘初集体下跌，创业板开盘跌近5%，盘中股指跌幅有所收窄，午前再度回落，创业板跌3.5%。算力硬件普遍陷入调整，光模块、光芯片、光通信等集体走低，“易中天”早盘跌幅均一度超过10%。光伏、新能源、电力、农业等板块逆势上涨。 港股同样低开，恒指、恒科指早盘跌幅一度收窄，午盘跌幅再度扩大，恒指、恒科指双双跌1%，科网股集体下跌，百度、腾讯、阿里跌幅居前。AI硬件股继续下挫，中际旭创、剑桥科技、长飞光纤光缆跌幅一度均超过10%。债市方面，国债期货多数上涨。商品方面，国内商品期货多数下跌。核心市场走势： A股 ：截至发稿，沪指跌1.14%，深成指跌2.22%，创业板指跌3.50%。 港股 ：截至发稿，恒指跌1.06%，恒科指跌1.75%。 债市 ：国债期货全线上涨，截至发稿，30年期主力合约涨0.28%，10年期主力合约涨0.07%，5年期主力合约涨0.02%，2年期主力合约持平。银行间主要利率债收益率普遍下行，10年期国债“26附息国债16”收益率下行1.05bp报1.5780%， 创历史新低 ；30年期国债“26超长特别国债04”收益率下行1.4bp报2.0360%， 创2025年8月26日以来新低。 商品 ：国内商品期货多数下跌，截至发稿，化工品跌幅居前，聚乙烯跌3.90%；能源品涨跌参半，跌3.40%；农副产品多数下跌，鸡蛋跌3.06%；基本金属涨跌参半，锡跌3.04%；油脂油料全部下跌，菜油跌2.22%；贵金属多数下跌，白银跌1.45%；航运期货全部下跌，集运指数(欧线)跌1.00%；新能源材料多数下跌，工业硅跌0.93%；黑色系涨幅居前，焦炭涨2.75%；非金属建材涨跌参半，玻璃涨1.02%。 11:47 盘面上，个股跌多涨少，沪深京三市超4500股飘绿，上午半天成交1.13万亿。沪深两市半日成交额1.12万亿，较上个交易日缩量超过3400亿。板块方面，AI硬件侧盘初杀跌后出现反抽。传媒、农业板块活跃，银行、电信、公路、电力、家电、煤炭等红利板块走升。 具体来看，种子板块涨5.39%、居全行业涨幅榜第一，种植业涨3.48%、其他种植业涨2.41%。万向德农涨停、走出3天2板；新赛股份低开后拉至涨停；秋乐种业涨13.49%、天山生物涨11.85%、康农种业涨7.89%、神农种业涨7.14%、金健米业涨5.92%、敦煌种业涨5.74%。 逻辑上，农业的爆发是"官方数据+天气题材"双重催化。 其一，11月6日国家发展改革委"奋进'十五五'"系列新闻发布会披露：秋粮收购开局平稳、东北地区陆续上量，全国已累计收购秋粮1亿吨，进度与上年基本持平；随着粮食产能稳步提升，"十五五"时期每年粮食收购量将继续保持在4亿吨以上。 其二，天气端，受厄尔尼诺现象影响，亚洲大米基准价格升至近两年来的最高水平：泰国大米出口商协会数据显示，泰国5%碎米白米报价升至每吨499美元，为2024年12月以来最高，粮食安全题材情绪升温。 招商证券认为，2026年全球粮食供需边际收紧，厄尔尼诺、能源化肥供应及国际贸易扰动增加了粮食生产和流通的不确定性；国内粮食供给基础保持稳固，粮食增产正持续向单产提升和生产效率改善转变，带动种业、农资及种植环节升级。 电力电网板块集体拉升，新能股份、立新能源涨停、东方新能涨停；电网设备方向太阳电缆盘中直线涨停，灿能电力、华明装备、江苏华辰、神马电力、长高电气跟涨；华电辽能、乐山电力、南网科技、华能水电等绿电方向同步走强。 催化直接来自当日发改委发布会上国家能源局的"十五五"定调，信息密度极高：一是用电需求端，能源局发展规划司副司长葛炬表示，"十五五"时期在算力等新兴产业带动下，我国用电需求仍将刚性增长，预计年均增量将达到6000亿度左右，相当于每年新增3个上海市的用电量；同时建立电力供应充裕度预警机制，提出2030年电力供应充裕度大于1.1，即在用电负荷最高峰时刻仍有10%的保供能力余量。 平安证券表示，"十五五"时期全国算力用电量年均新增1000亿千瓦时以上，随着算力用电需求进一步增长以及绿电直连模式逐步落地，储能作为满足自发自用比例要求的重要设施，需求空间有望打开。算力需求与电力保供两条叙事在此交汇，使电力电网成为当日最"硬"的逆势主线。 光伏概念延续昨日强势，光伏电池组件板块午间涨1.56%。永臻股份涨停报20.74元、走出4连板；日出东方、安彩高科涨停；时创能源涨停；海源复材3连板；贝特利盘中涨超10%，金刚光伏、酉立智能、赛伍技术、钧达股份跟涨。 催化上，国家能源局数据显示2026年第三季度中国新增光伏装机约38.76GW，较2025年同期的28.06GW增长约38%，为2025年中以来首个同比正增长的季度，9月单月新增13.64GW、同比增长41.2%，需求端呈回暖态势。 华泰证券认为，2026年光伏设备行业的技术路线正在加速切换，BC技术加速导入地面电站场景，市场认可度持续提高。 银行板块逆势拉升，沪农商行涨2.54%，苏州银行涨1.71%、成都银行涨1.56%、江苏银行涨1.44%，建设银行、渝农商行跟涨；保险、铁路公路同步走强——在指数跌超1%的早盘，低估值高股息资产是典型的避险承接。 另一个亮点藏在半导体板块内部：板块整体领跌，但设备与代工环节震荡回暖，华虹宏力涨8.37%，盘中一度涨超10%、京仪装备涨5.53%（盘中一度涨超10%），中科飞测、富创精密、盛美上海、华峰测控、芯源微跟涨。 催化包括11月5日在深圳举行的中荷出口管制对话机制第九次会议——双方同意加强对话交流，共同努力维护半导体等产业链供应链稳定畅通（商务部），外围管制恐慌阶段性缓和，自主可控资金回流设备环节。 与美股AI硬件链深度绑定的算力硬件板块开盘即领跌：东山精密、剑桥科技、澳弘电子竞价跌停，中际旭创、新易盛、天孚通信等开盘跌超10%。 中际旭创、新易盛、立讯精密、东山精密、天孚通信、海光信息等上市公司纷纷在午间发布公告，表态将充分运用政策工具，通过回购等方式，维护公司价值和广大投资者利益。 10:36 华虹宏力涨超10%，中微公司、中芯国际走升，科创综指、科创50明显收窄跌幅。 10:11 市场资金逐渐流入红利阵营，中国移动、中国电信、长江电力、牧原股份、美的集团、格力电器、宁沪高速、中国神华、建设银行等走强。 09:46 农业板块连续拉抬，万向德农涨停，秋乐种业、康农种业、神农种业、敦煌种业大涨。 消息面上，水利部回应“史上最强厄尔尼诺”：明年防汛形势更严峻。 A股光伏板块逆势拉升，永臻股份4连板，贝特利、时创能源涨超10%，酉立智能、金刚光伏、赛伍技术、钧达股份跟涨。 09:31 A股半导体芯片股集体下挫，普冉股份、和林微纳、芯海科技、澜起科技跌超10%，君正股份、晶丰明源、盛科通信、兆易创新等跌超8%。 算力硬件股开盘领跌，东山精密、剑桥科技、澳弘电子等跌停，中际旭创、新易盛、天孚通信、迅捷兴、满坤科技等多股跌超10%。 09:27 上证指数低开2.11%，创业板指跌4.99%。AI硬件侧领跌，中际旭创跌超12%。保险、银行板块逆市活跃。 09:21 articles.title: 隔夜美股崩盘：一场由1000亿美元“抢跑”引爆的反身性风暴
articles.summary: 周四，高盛的电话机要爆炸了。 “痛苦程度极高。” 这是高盛顶级股票交易员John Flood在周四当日报告中给客户发的一句话。他的电话机，用他自己的话说，“正在爆炸”。 纳斯达克100指数周四收跌6.4%，单日蒸发市值约2.3万亿美元，创2020年3月以来最大单日跌幅。标普500跌4.4%，费城半导体指数暴跌12%。“恐慌指数”VIX飙升70%，英伟达年内涨幅悉数回吐，闪迪单日暴跌22%。 触发这场崩盘的直接导火索，是民主党在中期选举中横扫国会两院。高盛随即警告，此次“蓝色海啸”将导致约45%的美国计划数据中心扩张容量面临暂停令——支撑AI科技股估值的核心叙事，在一夜之间被政治现实打了一个问号。 但行情的惨烈程度，远超政策冲击本身所能解释的范围。 野村证券衍生品策略师Charlie McElligott在周四盘中发布的一份报告里， 给出了另一层解释——这场崩盘，有相当一部分是被“最聪明的那群人”自己踩出来的。 McElligott描述了一个市场悖论：周四美股盘中，当摩根士丹利中午算出520亿美元的收盘前机械卖单并整个华尔街人人皆知后，所有人都试图提前卖出等低点买回，结果抢跑者自己变成了推动下跌的力量。他警告，若惯常的“下午2-3点低点然后反弹”没有出现，抢跑者自己也会变成推动下跌的力量。果然，当天收盘一片惨烈。叠加杠杆ETF 470亿、波动率控制基金610亿及dealer负gamma，总机械卖压超1000亿美元，且周五仍将持续。 而今天亚太市场，韩国和日本的暴跌正在回答这一问题。 一笔1000亿美元的定时炸弹，整个华尔街都知道 要理解McElligott的逻辑，先要理解一个机制。 市场上有一类产品叫 杠杆ETF ，比如“两倍做多纳斯达克”。它们每天收盘前必须做一件事：把当天的盈亏重新平衡回目标杠杆比例。 当市场大跌时，这意味着它们必须在收盘前卖出大量股票——跌得越惨，卖得越多，这是被动的、机械的、不可避免的。 还有一类叫 波动率控制基金（Vol Control） ，当市场波动率飙升时，它们会系统性地降低股票仓位——同样是机械的，且通常滞后一到两天执行。 周四，这两股力量叠加在一起，规模大得吓人。 摩根士丹利衍生品团队在当地时间11月5日中午算出：假设价格维持在下午1点的水平，收盘前杠杆ETF的被迫卖出规模约为 520亿美元 。其中仅半导体一个板块就要吃掉210亿，纳斯达克100再吃150亿。 野村的McElligott给出的数字略低，但同样触目惊心：杠杆ETF约 470亿美元 ，这是野村数据库中有史以来第二大的单日再平衡规模，仅次于今年6月5日的513亿美元。他补充说，这笔卖单“格外痛苦”，因为其中86%的资产集中在科技和AI相关标的。 叠加约 610亿美元 的波动率控制基金卖单，以及dealer负gamma每下跌1%带来的约 70亿美元 卖压，全市场机械性供给轻松超过 1000亿美元 。 这些数字的关键特性是： 它们是可以被提前计算出来的。 摩根士丹利中午算出520亿这个数字之后，用McElligott的话说， “在华尔街，没有任何信息能保密超过45分钟” ——这个数字迅速“整个华尔街皆知”。 聪明钱的如意算盘：提前卖，等低点，买回来 知道了这笔机械卖单，交易员们的反应是什么？ McElligott称， 主动交易者面对这类机械流，通常会尝试“抢跑”。 逻辑很简单： 既然收盘前会有一波大规模被动抛售，那我现在就卖，等它砸完了再低价买回来。 而且这个策略最近一直有效。McElligott在报告中指出，在近期几次"单日大幅波动"的交易日里，市场往往会在美东时间盘中 下午2点到3点 之间形成当日低点，随后抢跑者和对冲盘开始翻转、止盈、平仓，推动市场在收盘前反弹，最终收盘价高于那笔“预期中的”机械抛售所隐含的极值。 就在上周四，McElligott刚刚提醒过市场“又来了”——当时杠杆ETF面临350亿美元的卖单，最后市场也走出了 “2-3点低点+收盘反弹” 的经典结构。 今年6月韩国市场崩盘那次，美股也是类似的剧本。 4月关税暂停那天，这个机制反向运转：McElligott测算出历史最大的 +343亿美元 收盘前买入再平衡，抢跑者提前买，最终推动市场大涨。 所以周四，当摩根士丹利的520亿美元数字在中午传遍全街，每一个知道这个数字的交易员脑子里都在盘算同一件事： 现在卖，等下午2-3点的低点，然后买回来。 反身性的陷阱：骑兵就是那个在卖的人 然后McElligott在报告里写下了那个让人后背发凉的担忧： “如果那个'假设中的下午2-3点低点然后反弹'根本没有出现，怎么办？” 显然，现在可怕的地方在于：这些数字大到‘万一’我们没有出现那个几乎被视为理所当然的尾盘‘先见低点再反弹’（从低点反弹标准的一两个百分点），无法在下午2到3点的‘标准TWAP’窗口反弹、反而创出新低…… 而是在对市场‘会在最后一小时反弹’的假设虚晃一枪之后，收在最低点。 这正是反身性悖论的核心。 当所有人都知道同一个剧本，并且同时按剧本行动时，剧本本身就失效了。 原本应该集中在收盘前发生的1000亿美元机械卖单，被提前“抢跑”的主动交易者分散到了全天——这些抢跑者自己，就成了推动市场下跌的力量。 与此同时，波动率控制基金的卖单还有一到两天的滞后——周四的暴跌，会触发这类基金在 周五 继续卖出。McElligott写道，当天下午3点跌幅对应的波动率控制卖出量约为 610亿美元 ，若跌幅扩大到10%，这个数字会膨胀到 700亿美元 。 更致命的是：当所有抢跑者都已经卖出，在等着“那个低点”的时候—— 谁来接盘？ McElligott在报告里用了一个meme来描述这个场景：所有人都坐在椅子上，等着同一个反弹——但椅子不够。 ZeroHedge分析总结道： “有时候骑兵在下午3点到来。有时候，骑兵就是那个在卖的人。” 周四，骑兵没有来。市场以全日最低点收盘：纳指100跌6.4%，标普500跌4.4% 踩踏现场：年度最佳交易在48小时内被扫倒 在反身性机制引爆之前，市场上还有另一个火药桶在等待引线。 McElligott将今年华尔街的“年度最佳交易”称为“半导体-能源哑铃策略”——做多半导体（AI算力需求受益），同时做多能源（地缘风险溢价+通胀对冲）。这个策略在几周前的累计回报高达66%，夏普比率3.3。 然后，在过去48小时里，两条腿同时被扫倒： 能源：本周下跌 10.2% 半导体：本周下跌 13.1% 周夏普比率分别为 -17.2 和 -10.1 。 能源腿的崩塌，来自市场对伊朗局势的重新定价——McElligott观察到白宫释放出可能在伊朗问题上“松口”的信号，战争溢价被迅速抽走，布伦特原油本周跌幅创新冠疫情以来最大。 半导体腿的崩塌，来自民主党横扫国会后市场对数据中心监管的担忧。 两个方向同时崩，持有哑铃策略的基金面临的不仅是亏损，而是 被迫平仓 。McElligott描述的“保住今年收益、活着进入明年”的心态，在这个时刻被彻底击穿。 Walleye资本当天宣布返还客户资金并解雇股票部门负责人，称这是新冠疫情以来最惨的一个月。高盛交易员John Flood描述做多机构“再度陷入僵局”，昨天反弹中买入的超大规模云计算仓位被迅速抛出， “目前尚未看到买家入场接盘”。 ETF层面的异常成交量印证了恐慌程度：SPY成交量较20日均值高出160%，QQQ高出100%，半导体ETF SMH高出150%。 据Vanda Research高级股票策略师Jai Malhi，周四零售投资者的卖出规模“有望成为自去年7月底以来最大的一次散户清仓”。 债券被轧空，另一条腿也在流血 还有一条被忽视的腿在同时断裂。 CTA趋势基金在今年积累了大量债券空头仓位，这是“做空债券/做多通胀”交易的一部分，也是哑铃策略的隐性配套。 股市崩盘触发了避险买盘涌入债市，美债价格急涨，债券空头被迫平仓。McElligott的测算显示，CTA在债券方向面临“大规模轧空”：若美债价格再涨2%，将触发约 2250亿美元 的全球债券被迫买入，其中美国2年期债券约485亿美元，欧元区2年期约695亿美元，日本10年期约239亿美元。 这意味着，债券空头的轧空本身也在成为推动债市上涨、进一步压缩股票多头的力量——又一个反身性循环。 崩盘还没结束：周五的滞后卖压 周四收盘，并不意味着这轮机械性卖压的结束。 波动率控制基金的执行存在滞后。McElligott写道，周四的市场跌幅，会在周五继续触发这类基金的卖单——“今天的跌幅正在进一步加载进队列”。 瑞银的估算更为直接：其风险控制再平衡模型显示，若标普500下跌2%，系统性基金的卖出规模将达到 950亿至1050亿美元 。 亚洲市场已经在回答这个问题了。 周五早盘，韩国综合指数暴跌8.8%，跌破5000点关口并触发熔断机制 ——这个点位曾被韩国总统李在明视为经济复苏的里程碑，如今迅速跌穿。日经225指数跌近5.8%，盘中跌破6万点，自6月高点回落超过20%，正式进入技术性熊市。 美股期货在亚洲早盘出现小幅反弹，纳斯达克期货一度翻绿，显示部分投资者开始逢低介入。但瑞银警告，系统性卖出的压力尚未完全释放。 周五还有一个变量：美国10月非农就业报告将于当天出炉，市场共识预期为新增就业5.9万人，失业率维持在4.2%。数据的方向，将决定这轮调整能否找到喘息的窗口。 风险提示及免责条款
